subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 70-year-old woman with open-angle glaucoma is prescribed topical timolol after prostaglandin drops fail to control her intraocular pressure.
question: Which of the following best describes how timolol lowers intraocular pressure?

options.text: Decreases production of aqueous humor through β-blockade of the ciliary epithelium
Increases outflow of aqueous humor through the trabecular meshwork via α1 blockade
Increases uveoscleral outflow via prostaglandin analog activity
Decreases aqueous humor production by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase
Constricts the pupillary sphincter through muscarinic agonism

explanation_correct: Timolol is a nonselective β-blocker used for glaucoma; β-blockade decreases the production of aqueous humor by the ciliary epithelium, lowering intraocular pressure. Propranolol, timolol, and nadolol are the classic nonselective β-blockers (N to Z).

explanation_incorrect.B: Increasing trabecular outflow via α1 effects is not the mechanism of β-blockers; α1 agonists such as phenylephrine produce mydriasis instead.
explanation_incorrect.C: Increased uveoscleral outflow is the mechanism of prostaglandin analogs, not timolol.
explanation_incorrect.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition describes dorzolamide/acetazolamide, a different glaucoma drug class.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pupillary sphincter constriction describes pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist used in glaucoma.

educationalObjective: Timolol lowers intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor production.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 62-year-old man with a reduced ejection fraction of 28% is being discharged after an episode of acute decompensated heart failure. His physician selects a β-blocker proven to curb mortality in heart failure by blocking neurohormonal stress and preventing deleterious cardiac remodeling.
question: Which of the following sets of β-blockers is appropriate for this patient?

options.text: Propranolol, timolol, and nadolol
Atenolol, betaxolol, and esmolol
Bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol
Nebivolol, labetalol, and timolol
Esmolol, nadolol, and betaxolol

explanation_correct: In heart failure, β-blockade of neurohormonal stress prevents deleterious cardiac remodeling and decreases mortality. The three β-blockers shown to curb mortality in HF are bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol — this is a classic First Aid association.

explanation_incorrect.A: Propranolol, timolol, and nadolol are nonselective β-blockers (N to Z) used for glaucoma, hyperthyroidism, and variceal bleeding prophylaxis, not the mortality-proven HF agents.
explanation_incorrect.B: Atenolol and betaxolol are β1-selective agents used for hypertension and glaucoma; esmolol is for SVT — none of these three are the canonical HF mortality drugs.
explanation_incorrect.D: Nebivolol combines β1 blockade with β3-mediated NO release; labetalol is a mixed α/β-blocker used in hypertensive emergencies; timolol is for glaucoma — not the standard HF trio.
explanation_incorrect.E: Esmolol (short-acting, SVT), nadolol (variceal bleeding, nonselective), and betaxolol (glaucoma) are not the HF mortality-proven combination.

educationalObjective: Bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol are the β-blockers proven to reduce mortality in heart failure.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 71-year-old woman in the ICU develops new-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. The team wants an intravenous agent with an extremely short half-life so it can be titrated or stopped quickly as her rhythm evolves.
question: Which β-blocker is most appropriate, and what is its mechanism of action in this arrhythmia?

options.text: Propranolol; increases AV conduction velocity through class III effects
Nadolol; decreases hepatic venous pressure gradient
Atenolol; increases contractility through β1 blockade
Betaxolol; decreases aqueous humor production
Esmolol; decreases AV conduction velocity as a class II antiarrhythmic

explanation_correct: Esmolol and metoprolol are the β-blockers used for supraventricular tachycardia (eg, atrial fibrillation), where β1-blockade decreases AV conduction velocity — the class II antiarrhythmic effect. Esmolol's ultrashort duration makes it ideal for rapid titration in unstable settings.

explanation_incorrect.A: Propranolol is nonselective and does not increase AV conduction; β-blockers decrease AV conduction velocity.
explanation_incorrect.B: Nadolol is used prophylactically for variceal bleeding by reducing portal hypertension, not for acute rate control.
explanation_incorrect.C: β1-blockade decreases contractility, not increases it; atenolol is not the short-acting ICU agent described.
explanation_incorrect.D: Decreased aqueous humor production is timolol's glaucoma mechanism, not an antiarrhythmic action.

educationalObjective: Metoprolol and esmolol treat SVT by decreasing AV conduction velocity (class II antiarrhythmic action).

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has endoscopic evidence of medium-sized esophageal varices without prior bleeding. His gastroenterologist starts prophylactic therapy to reduce hepatic venous pressure gradient and portal hypertension.
question: Which β-blocker is an appropriate prophylactic choice for this indication?

options.text: Esmolol
Nadolol
Metoprolol
Betaxolol
Atenolol

explanation_correct: β-blockers reduce hepatic venous pressure gradient and portal hypertension for prophylaxis against variceal bleeding. Nadolol, propranolol, and carvedilol are the agents used for no portal circulation — nadolol (nonselective, β1 = β2) is a classic choice.

explanation_incorrect.A: Esmolol is an ultrashort-acting β1-selective agent used for supraventricular tachycardia, not variceal prophylaxis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Metoprolol is β1-selective and is used for heart failure, hypertension, MI, and SVT — not variceal bleeding prophylaxis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Betaxolol is β1-selective and used for glaucoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Atenolol is β1-selective and used for hypertension and angina; variceal prophylaxis requires nonselective agents.

educationalObjective: Nadolol, propranolol, and carvedilol are the β-blockers used prophylactically for variceal bleeding.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A medical student is reviewing β-blocker selectivity and recalls that selective β1-antagonists mostly go from A to M in the alphabet while nonselective β-antagonists mostly go from N to Z.
question: Which of the following correctly matches a β-blocker with its receptor pharmacology?

options.text: Carvedilol — β1-selective antagonist used in glaucoma
Propranolol — β1-selective antagonist used in heart failure mortality reduction
Nebivolol — combines cardiac-selective β1-blockade with β3-receptor stimulation that increases nitric oxide and decreases SVR
Nadolol — nonselective α- and β-antagonist with modified suffix
Labetalol — β2-selective antagonist used for asthma

explanation_correct: Nebivolol combines cardiac-selective β1-adrenergic blockade with stimulation of β3 receptors, which activate nitric oxide synthase in the vasculature and decrease systemic vascular resistance — "NebivOlol increases NO." This unique dual mechanism distinguishes it from the other β-blockers.

explanation_incorrect.A: Carvedilol is a nonselective β- and α-antagonist (with a modified suffix instead of "-olol") used in heart failure, not a β1-selective glaucoma agent.
explanation_incorrect.B: Propranolol is a nonselective β1 = β2 antagonist (N to Z group) used for hyperthyroidism, migraine, and variceal bleeding — not a β1-selective HF mortality drug.
explanation_incorrect.D: Nadolol is a nonselective β1 = β2 antagonist (not α- and β-); nonselective α- and β-antagonists are carvedilol and labetalol, which have modified suffixes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Labetalol is a nonselective α- and β-antagonist; β2-selective antagonists are not used for asthma — β-blockade can worsen asthma.

educationalObjective: Nebivolol = β1-selective blockade plus β3-mediated nitric oxide production that decreases SVR.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 54-year-old man with type 1 diabetes taking a β-blocker develops hypoglycemia after his insulin dose but does not notice his usual warning symptoms of tremor and anxiety until he becomes confused. He also reports new erectile dysfunction since starting the drug.
question: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for the patient's unrecognized hypoglycemia?

options.text: β-blockade masking adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia, such as tremor
β-blockade directly destroying pancreatic β cells and causing permanent insulin excess
β-blockade inducing dyslipidemia that impairs counterregulation of blood glucose
β-blockade blocking AV nodal conduction and decreasing glucose delivery to the brain
β-blockade increasing insulin clearance by the liver through α1 blockade

explanation_correct: Masked hypoglycemia is a listed adverse effect of β-blockers: blocking β-mediated adrenergic warning signs (tremor, tachycardia, anxiety) leaves patients — especially those with diabetes — unaware of falling glucose. Other β-blocker adverse effects include erectile dysfunction, bradycardia/AV block, CNS effects (seizures, sleep alterations), dyslipidemia (metoprolol), and asthma/COPD exacerbations.

explanation_incorrect.B: β-blockers do not destroy pancreatic β cells; they mask the adrenergic symptoms that normally warn of hypoglycemia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Dyslipidemia (seen with metoprolol) is a separate adverse effect and does not explain the loss of hypoglycemia warning symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.D: AV block is a distinct cardiovascular adverse effect and does not impair cerebral glucose delivery in hypoglycemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: β-blockers do not increase hepatic insulin clearance through α1 blockade; the issue is masking of adrenergic symptoms.

educationalObjective: β-blockers can mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (tremor, anxiety) in patients with diabetes.
